title: India's Chip Startups Are Heading to France. They Are Bringing Working Silicon, Not Slide Decks.
excerpt: VerveSemi, AGNIT Semiconductors, and Netrasemi have been selected for Bharat Innovates 2026 in Nice. All three are at or near production.
body:
Three Indian semiconductor startups have been selected to represent the country at Bharat Innovates 2026, a deep-tech showcase running June 14 to 16 in Nice, France. The companies — VerveSemi, AGNIT Semiconductors, and Netrasemi — are not sending prototypes or slide decks. They are bringing chips that are already in production or approaching it. The gap between India's semiconductor ambitions and its semiconductor capabilities is narrowing faster than most observers expected.

The selection was made under an initiative of the Ministry of Education and coordinated through YourStory's Bharat Project. The three companies cover distinctly different slices of the chip market, which is itself a signal of how broad India's emerging semiconductor ecosystem has become.

Netrasemi, based in Thiruvananthapuram, builds edge AI processors on RISC-V architecture. Its flagship chip, the Netra E2000, is designed for smart cameras, IoT devices, robotics, and surveillance systems — all manufactured on TSMC's 28nm process. The company raised 107 crore rupees in a Series A round in 2025 led by Zoho and Unicorn India Ventures, and its chips are already in the hands of three customers running pilots. Commercial volumes are expected by mid-2027. The platform, the company claims, can run more than 100 AI applications.

AGNIT Semiconductors operates in a more strategically sensitive space. The Bengaluru-based startup, founded by seven semiconductor experts with deep roots in IISc, specialises in gallium nitride technology — a material critical for defence applications including radar systems, electronic warfare jammers, and drone communication links. In 2023, the Ministry of Defence signed a contract with AGNIT for advanced GaN semiconductors for next-generation wireless transmitters. The company has three pilots running with defence public sector units and private defence firms, with volumes expected to reach 5,000 to 10,000 chips within nine months. Volume production is planned to begin by late 2026.

VerveSemi, headquartered in Greater Noida with operations in Bengaluru, focuses on analog and RF semiconductors — data converters, RF transceivers, and analog IP for aerospace, electric vehicles, defence, and industrial applications. The company has developed more than 110 inventions, produced 25 ready-to-deploy chips, and secured 10 patents. Its technology supports projects including ISRO's Gaganyaan program and EV inverter systems, achieving power efficiency improvements of up to five times in certain applications.

The backdrop to the France showcase is a larger shift in India's industrial policy. The India Semiconductor Mission, launched in December 2021, set the entire wave in motion. Two government schemes have done the heavy lifting: the Design Linked Incentive scheme, which supports chip design work, and the Production Linked Incentive scheme, which provides capital for manufacturing. Together, they have compressed a development timeline that typically takes three to four years into something significantly shorter.

The results are visible in adjacent sectors. The government's restrictions on uncertified internet-connected CCTV cameras effectively shut Chinese brands like Hikvision and Dahua out of the Indian market, opening a fresh opportunity for domestic chip manufacturers. Companies like Netrasemi and Mindgrove — another Indian chip startup backed by PeakXV Partners — are now building the processors that go inside the cameras that replaced them.

India still imports the overwhelming majority of the chips it uses. That will not change overnight. But the trajectory has shifted. The country now has startups designing chips for AI, defence, electric vehicles, and space exploration — and the government is willing to act as the first customer, which is the single most important thing a government can do to build a domestic semiconductor industry.

"We are working with a market opportunity that's real, not theoretical," said Jyothis Indirabhai, co-founder and CEO of Netrasemi. "AI has arrived, and the older generation of chips was never built for it. That opens a real opportunity for newcomers."

Pratap Narayan Singh of VerveSemi put it in simpler terms: India imports chips on a massive scale. Building at home is the natural next step. The three startups heading to Nice are proof that the step is already being taken.

*Sources: YourStory, Communications Today, Inc42, Engineers Garage*
